Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes (recorded)
Attendees: Alicia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Daniel Reyes (Velora CTO), Priya Nair (Velora Eng Mgr), Sam Ortiz (Velora Infra)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Deep technical session about autoscaling strategy for Velora's V1 inference workload, discussion of queueing models, burst policies, reserved GPU sizing, and tradeoffs around latency vs cost. Action: Redwood to send capacity template and run benchmark using Velora traces.

Topics: autoscaling triggers, warm pools / reserved GPUs, burst policies, queueing/backpressure, KV cache behavior, batching/continuous batching, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem deployment nuances.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alicia Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros and then Marcus will jump in on the autoscale design.
[00:14] Daniel Reyes: Yep, hi, Daniel here. We're eager to understand how Redwood handles bursty clinical traffic and whether reserved GPUs plus bursts makes sense.
[00:24] Marcus Li: cool, thanks. I'll try to cover both the control plane signals we use for scaling and the runtime considerations — kv cache, batching, quantization — that change effective throughput. Apologies in advance for my coffee voice.
[00:36] Priya Nair: no worries. one ask up front: our latency SLO is 200ms p95 for short chat calls and 1s for longer context runs. We also have nightly bulk jobs.
[00:48] Marcus Li: okay that's useful. Two quick clarifying q's: what peak QPS do you see today and what's the expected burst multiple?
[00:56] Sam Ortiz: baseline is roughly 80 requests/sec for our chat endpoint, with spikes to ~650 for 2-5 minutes during morning syncs; plan to grow 2x in 3 months.
[01:10] Marcus Li: nice, that burst pattern is pretty typical. At a high level we recommend a two-tier approach: reserved GPUs sized for steady-state plus a burst pool with autoscaling/queueing to handle short spikes. We'll go through queueing model choices — basically whether to scale by GPU utilization or by queue length / token backlog.
[01:30] Daniel Reyes: what's the difference in terms of cold start or latency if you scale by utilization vs queue length?
[01:36] Marcus Li: good question. If you scale on GPU util you avoid spinning up for small jitters but you can see longer queuing when a sudden burst arrives because util is a lagging indicator. Scaling on queue length/token backlog triggers earlier; you'll provision before util rises but you may oscillate on noisy signals. We typically combine them with hysteresis: trigger when queue_length > X or avg_latency > Y for N seconds. Also we use a warm-pool concept — reserved GPUs stay warmed (no cold start), and burst nodes can be kept in a warm standby if the burst budget allows.
[02:12] Priya Nair: when you say warm pool, do you mean prewarmed containers on GPUs or actual reserved hardware? we wanted to avoid paying for idle HW.
[02:20] Marcus Li: warm pool can be configured either way. For Dedicated/Private customers you can reserve a small number of GPUs in a warm-standby mode — lower frequency housekeeping, kept ready — or use ephemeral burst instances in the cloud with a short spin-up time (30-90s). There's a cost tradeoff: reserved GPUs cost more but give consistent latency; ephemeral bursts are cheaper but have cold start tail.
[02:42] Sam Ortiz: our worry is the morning 5-min spikes — paying for full reserved capacity for those few minutes seems excessive. Any middle ground?
[02:50] Marcus Li: yes, that's where a burst credit model helps. You can reserve steady-state capacity for, say, 150 rps equivalent and configure burst capacity that uses pre-allocated burst credits to start warmed nodes quickly for short periods. Credits replenish over time. That reduces the need to permanently reserve for short bursts.
[03:08] Daniel Reyes: interesting. how do you size the reserved GPUs though? do you base it on token throughput per GPU?
[03:14] Marcus Li: exactly. We run per-model throughput benchmarks using realistic prompt sizes (tokens per request) and measure tokens/sec and latencies. For instance, on A100-ish class, a quantized 13B running 8k context at X config might do Y tokens/sec. We compute required GPUs = ceil(peak_tokens_per_sec / tokens_per_gpu). But also account for batching inefficiencies and KV cache hit rates.
[03:36] Priya Nair: explain KV cache impact — we use a lot of stateful chat, does that help?
[03:41] Marcus Li: KV cache is a huge factor. If a session can reuse KV cache across requests (prefix/turns), token work per request drops significantly because you don't re-run past tokens. That increases effective throughput and lowers cost. Caveat: KV cache requires sticky routing to the same host and memory per-session; if you scale out aggressively and route to different nodes you'll miss cache hits (sometimes transcribed as kv cash).
[04:05] Daniel Reyes: sticky routing — is that per user session? does that complicate failover?
[04:09] Marcus Li: it's per-session or per-conversation id. We support sticky routing policies with automatic fallback: if a node is unhealthy we can route to another node and rehydrate KV cache from prefix caching or from longer request context — that adds latency. Tradeoff: higher cache hit -> lower cost, but you need enough memory per node for cached sessions and strong routing.
[04:30] Sam Ortiz: memory for kv cache — how much? we have many long conversations, 10k tokens per session sometimes.
[04:36] Marcus Li: memory grows with total KV size across active sessions. For 10k tokens session, kv footprint depends on model and quantization; rough ballpark: a few hundred MB per long session for large models if uncompressed. We recommend eviction policies and session TTLs. For heavy stateful workloads, plan reserved nodes with larger GPU memory or use model quantization to reduce KV size.
[04:59] Priya Nair: speaking of quantization, what's Redwood's stance — 4-bit vs 8-bit tradeoffs?
[05:05] Marcus Li: 4-bit QLoRA/quant aims for the best cost but can sometimes degrade accuracy or change latency profiles. 8-bit is safer for parity with FP16 but still gives benefits. On our benchmarking we provide model-specific perf/quality curves so you can choose. For mission-critical clinical outputs we often advise 8-bit or a tuned 4-bit profile plus evals.
[05:28] Daniel Reyes: ok. can you walk through an example queueing model we'd use? we want something simple we can reason about.
[05:34] Marcus Li: Sure. For simple reasoning we use an M/M/c style intuition: arrival process (roughly Poisson-ish for aggregated traffic), service rate per GPU (tokens/sec mapped to requests/sec given average prompt size), and c servers (GPUs). You can compute probability of queueing and expected wait. In practice arrivals are bursty so we also look at peak percentiles and tail latency via simulation. Redwood's autoscaler can use queue depth thresholds and predicted service time to pre-scale.
[06:06] Priya Nair: predicted service time — is that stable with dynamic batching?
[06:10] Marcus Li: dynamic batching increases throughput but introduces some batching delay. Continuous batching designs push small waits to batch many requests; this helps throughput but increases p95 slightly. We calibrate target batch sizes and max latency budget per request type. For example, we might cap batching delay to 25ms for interactive calls to keep within your 200ms p95.
[06:30] Sam Ortiz: any advice on telemetry signals we should expose to make autoscaler smarter?
[06:34] Marcus Li: yes: queue length, avg and p95 request latency, average tokens per request, token backlog, GPU utilization, and sample tracing from sticky sessions (cache hit rates). Also the rate of session stickiness changes. For private deployments, exposing node health and memory pressure for kv cache is helpful.
[06:55] Daniel Reyes: security/compliance concern — if we're on VPC or on-prem, can Redwood still do autoscaling bursting into public clouds? we need to meet data residency rules.
[07:03] Alicia Park: short answer: depends on deployment. For Private (VPC/on-prem) we can configure burst into a customer-approved cloud region or partner region, or keep bursts entirely within customer's VPC if they provision capacity. We also support a wholly on-prem model where Redwood control plane runs in customer VPC and compute stays inside their network. We'll share the deployment matrix.
[07:22] Priya Nair: ok good. audit logs, SSO, KMS — we'll need docs.
[07:27] Alicia Park: yes we'll attach SOC2 docs, KMS integration guides, and the SAML/SSO configuration doc in the follow-up.
[07:34] Marcus Li: back to sizing — one practical approach: run a small benchmark using your sample trace across three configs: baseline (no quant), 8-bit, and 4-bit, measure tokens/sec and p95, then compute GPUs needed for steady-state and peak. We'll show you the cost delta and expected p95 impact.
[07:53] Daniel Reyes: how long to run the benchmark?
[07:55] Marcus Li: typically 1-2 hours to cover variability; we can do a quick 20-min smoke run to validate config. Longer runs useful for tail behaviors and cache warmup.
[08:06] Priya Nair: sample data — any constraints for us sharing traces? we can't share PHI.
[08:11] Alicia Park: please scrub PHI; we accept synthetic or obfuscated traces. Marcus can provide a template for expected fields (timestamps, prompt size, session id) so you can map without PHI.
[08:21] Marcus Li: yes I'll share the trace schema. Also a note on queuing: if you have a high fraction of long-context requests (multi-k token), they can block throughput because they take longer service time; it's often worth isolating long-batch jobs into separate queue/route or using dedicated nodes for bulk processing to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[08:42] Sam Ortiz: for nightly bulk jobs, we do lower-priority batch work. can Redwood do prioritized queues?
[08:47] Marcus Li: yes, Redwood supports multi-queue priorities; low-priority jobs can be throttled or drained onto separate hardware. That way interactive traffic keeps latency SLO while bulk runs use spare cycles.
[08:58] Daniel Reyes: any tips for warm/cold cache rehydration to minimize latency if failover occurs?
[09:03] Marcus Li: prefetching recent tokens to a shared fast store isn't ideal because of size; instead we do lightweight checkpointing of session summaries or short prefix replays. If a node dies we can route and replay a short prefix (not the whole 10k) to rehydrate enough to serve next turn with minimal latency impact. There's tradeoffs between rehydration cost and storage complexity.
[09:22] Priya Nair: Are there known limits on number of sticky sessions per GPU?
[09:26] Marcus Li: depends on KV footprint. If typical session small, thousands of sessions per GPU possible. For long 10k-token sessions, it's lower. We'll help model that for your expected active sessions.
[09:36] Sam Ortiz: can we see an example capacity plan? like a table: steady rps -> reserved gpus -> burst pool size -> expected p95?
[09:43] Marcus Li: absolutely, we'll send the capacity planning template. It has columns for average tokens/request, avg requests/sec, desired p95, model throughput, GPUs recommended, buffer for cache misses, burst capacity, and cost estimates.
[09:58] Alicia Park: quick interjection — I want to call out the ops story: we'll provide runbooks for scaling events, and a recommended canary rollout for any model or quant change since that can affect latency/throughput profile.
[10:10] Daniel Reyes: good point. our compliance folks will want rollback steps and audit trails.
[10:15] Alicia Park: yep we'll include automatic fallback policies — e.g., if quantized model regresses on quality checks, traffic can fallback to FP16 variant. We log rollouts.
[10:24] Marcus Li: one more technical nuance: batching efficiency often depends on request size distribution. If most requests are one-liners you'll get high batching efficiency; varied sizes can reduce effective tokens/sec because of stragglers. We sometimes use size-based queues to improve packing efficiency.
[10:43] Priya Nair: Uh, when you say size-based queues, is that complexity we need to operate?
[10:48] Marcus Li: Redwood manages it in the runtime; you just define the routing rules. For example, small interactive requests go to interactive pool with a stricter batch latency cap; large long-context runs go to a separate pool optimized for throughput.
[11:02] Daniel Reyes: any gotchas when using quantization for KV cache size?
[11:06] Marcus Li: yes, quantization affects memory layout and may reduce KV footprint, but some Q configs require reformatting which can change warmup times. We'll show the measured rehydration times for the quant profiles in the benchmark.
[11:18] Sam Ortiz: let's cover failover: if an AZ goes down, do you auto-fallback to another region? how's data residency handled?
[11:24] Marcus Li: for Hosted it's cross-region fallback; for Private you can restrict failover within your VPC/region. If cross-region fallback is needed we recommend encryption and KMS keys scoped appropriately and an approved DR plan. We'll include options in the follow-up doc.
[11:39] Daniel Reyes: timeline — if we decide to pilot, how long to stand up reserved GPUs + run benchmark?
[11:44] Alicia Park: pilot timeline: 1) sign order for pilot capacity (a week), 2) provision reserved nodes (1-3 days), 3) benchmark + tweak (1 week), total ~2-3 weeks depending on approvals.
[11:57] Priya Nair: budget — any rough numbers to prep?
[12:00] Alicia Park: we'll send a price range in the capacity plan. Example: steady 150 rps equivalent might map to N GPUs at $X/month; bursts priced separately. I'll include both cloud-equivalent and on-prem licensing.
[12:12] Daniel Reyes: perfect.
[12:15] Marcus Li: ok I'll summarize the technical recommendations: 1) size reserved GPUs for steady-state based on tokens/sec benchmarks, 2) enable a modest warm-pool and burst credits for short spikes, 3) use queue-length + latency triggers with hysteresis and a short pre-scale window (30s), 4) isolate long-context bulk jobs to separate pool, 5) instrument cache hit rate and token backlog as autoscaler signals, 6) run benchmarks across quant configs and pick the profile that meets quality/latency tradeoff.
[12:50] Priya Nair: that sounds good. can you also recommend initial numbers? like if we aim to handle 650 peak with p95 200ms — any guess?
[12:57] Marcus Li: ballpark: assuming avg prompt 120 tokens and interactive model does ~2000 tokens/sec per GPU in 8-bit with good batching, that is ~16 requests/sec per GPU. To handle 650 rps you'd need ~41 GPUs — but with KV cache and batching you might reduce that significantly; if cache hit 60% and batching effective, maybe down to mid-20s. We'll compute precisely in the capacity plan using your real traces.
[13:22] Daniel Reyes: good to have a concrete estimate.
[13:25] Alicia Park: ok wrapping up, recap and action items.
[13:28] Alicia Park: next steps — I'll send capacity template and pricing; Marcus will send benchmark config, SOC2 and VPC/on-prem docs; Daniel to share scrubbed traces. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff once traces are in.
[13:43] Daniel Reyes: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[13:46] Priya Nair: thanks.
[13:47] Sam Ortiz: thanks.
[13:48] Marcus Li: thanks all.
